appendix_q.overview: The printed proofs differ in completeness. Those of Sections A to G and of Appendix O, and the deduction of Theorem L.1 in Section L, are meant to be complete, if terse. The proofs of Proposition I.1, Theorem H.2(d), (e), Theorem J.3 and Proposition N.4 describe machines and programs and account for their sizes and running times. That these do exactly what is claimed can be verified only in the Lean development, and each of these four statements is followed by a formalization note that says so. Consequently the contracting case, and with it every main result, rests on Lean at these points.
routes: In Proposition K.5, Theorem K.6 and Proposition N.4 some printed references are to definitions or enter as standing hypotheses. Proposition N.4 repeats the iteration of Proposition K.5, as printed.
Lemma K.3, Theorem M.3 and Theorem N.5 use the general forms for families that are complete for grid sums, of which Corollary E.2 and the statements about the permanent are instances.
Proposition E.10 uses the step prop_flat_lower_sum of the proof of Proposition E.5, not the proposition. Lemma N.2 repeats the argument of Lemma M.1 on coefficients.

Theorem N.5 does not cite Lemma K.3, Theorem K.7 and Theorem M.3. Instead it uses the step thm_allfields_exceeds of the proof of the last of them and approximate analogues of the first two, which share their steps with them; the analogues are lem_circuit_approx and contracting_approx_complete. On the way the constants are cut off twice.

Of Lemma A.2 only the clauses that say that dφ is a pseudometric are taken from the lemma: the power law and dφ ≤ 1 come from its named parts, and the bound by a tree is used nowhere. The clause of Lemma K.4 on the size is never cited and is proved again where it is needed. Part (d) of Lemma C.4 is redundant where it is used. The form of the constants in Lemma N.2 is derived again in the proof of Theorem N.5.
Theorem H.2 uses parts (a) and (b) of Proposition H.1 through the named theorems that also prove the proposition.

figure1.caption: The structure of the proof. The two arrows marked P are the only steps that use the permanent; they use the circuit too, but only by substituting into it. The two arrows marked C are the only steps that look inside the circuit, both times at the polynomial at every gate. In the shaded boxes neither the polynomial that is to be computed nor a circuit occurs; the dashed boxes are the assumptions. For the determinant the arrows P are missing, and a Boolean circuit does not pass the arrows C (Section 2.5).

In the file printed in Section 3 circuits and the classes VP and VNP are defined over commutativesemirings. Thepermanentiswrittenthereas ∑ σ ∏ i xσ(i),i, whereSection1 has xi,σ(i); the two sums agree, as one sees by replacing σ with its inverse.

Lean defines the projection to the fixed points of a window (Section F) as the barycenter of the orbit, and projection_nearest shows that this is the nearest point. In the proof of Theorem F.6 the space of functions carries the sum where the text has the mean, which is one scaling factor. Lean states Lemma F.3 for explicit numbers, θn = 18⌈log2 n⌉ μ(L + 1)sL with L = ⌊logμ 2⌈log2 n⌉⌋ (kappa), which are not those of the printed proof, and C(n) in (F.1) and in Lemmas F.4 and F.5 is formed with them.
The families of tensors in Theorem A.6 and of maps in Proposition A.7 are indexed by any finite set.

A variable of block a of fk,ℓ is indexed by k strings, and the one at the place a is 0 in the variables that occur. The circuit sizes are the same, and the theorems with suffix _printed state Lemma E.3 and Propositions E.5 and E.10 for the printed polynomial.

Lemmas A.3, E.4, E.7, F.1, F.2, I.2, K.3, M.1, N.2 and N.3 and Proposition B.2 are proved in stronger or more general forms. For example, lem_hubs pushes the tensor t forward along an arbitrary map from its parties to a finite set of parties, of which o1, o2 are any two, and lem_hubs_further is the form with two further parties. Proposition B.2 is proved without the assumption that Σ1 and Σ2 are nonempty. Lemma E.4 is proved over every commutative semiring, and Lemmas E.7 and N.3 whenever t is covered by T1, . . . , TJ , so that linear maps may also be applied at the parties of P . In Section F Lemma F.1 is proved without the assumption s2 < μ and also for r = 0, and Lemma F.2 without the conditions 1 ≤ k < n and ξ, ω ≠ 0. Lemma K.3 is proved for every family that is complete for grid sums (Appendix M) and for every H ≥ 32. Lemmas M.1 and N.2 are proved with any algebraically closed field of characteristic p in the place of K. The flat bound for approximating circuits has 14 where Proposition E.10 has 16.

Laws may have any finite sets of elements, slots and channels. A law in Lean also records that its channels connect its elements, in the form that indices which agree along all channels agree everywhere; on Uh, where the channels are all the edges, this holds by itself. The conditions on λ, on ℐ and on Uh come with Theorem G.2. Its Lean form also states the choices of Section G: u and C0 are as in Theorem F.6, C′ 0 ≥ 2C0 +1 is an integer and C1 = 4C′ 0. It asserts that some multiple h ≥ 2u of u satisfies (G.1), and it asserts (a) and (b) for every such h. That the channels there are the edges, each once, on which the norm in Theorem G.2(b) depends, follows from the definitions but is stated by no theorem of the development. The theorem def_law lists only three of the fields of the structure, in one direction, so that it rests on reading the structure that it is the printed notion.

In Proposition H.1, the set V0 is only stated to have as many elements as Gn, bijectivity on cosets is stated as equivariance and freeness, and the cosets over a coset are given by representatives (prop_tower_representatives: there is exactly one in each coset). Lean states the proposition for every h ≥ 3 and every n ≥ 0.

Theorem H.2 and Proposition J.2 state their clauses as the fields of structures. A relay is a law with one slot, two channels, one index and λ = 0, applied to a batch of packets. Thus relays too have outcomes and leave copies and dead packets at the ends of their strings, an outcome of a relay is good if it equals the number of packets of the batch on both channels, and there is a law move for every stage, type, coset and law, with t = 0 for those not chosen. The value of a tree is written as a sum, over the contents of named packets, present or absent, of products of the values of its nodes, and no theorem restates this as the value of a network as defined in Section H. As printed in (b) and (e), the dead packets are a set of names that are not all stated to be present, so that the bound on what a node ever holds may count absent ones. The end packets of relays count as dead, and in networks without these packets they would count among the absent ones. In part (e) Lean has the constant C of the theorem, and it counts for every move at p, with the number t, also t times one plus the number of its slots at p, which covers the zeros in slots. Proposition J.2 uses only the total M C . Packets have a direction in Lean, and packets from a node to itself are allowed and stay at their node. The programs may depend on M , N , ℓ, the ring of the network and the bound on the number of given nodes, respectively on v, T , k, the automaton and the standing data. In Proposition J.2 the outcomes range over tuples of numbers below a bound that is part of the data (the field U1); no clause says that every good outcome lies below it, and the identity sums over those that do. Whether an outcome is good is tested with the integer ⌊2C1a2 1⌋ (thm_tree_good). This implies the printed notion and is equal to it when 2C1a2 1 is an integer, as the laws provide.

Proposition J.2 is proved without the bound on lg T , and its number of bits in all counts every copy ever held and the zeros in slots. Its sum runs over the numbers of packets with at most N packets at each node, as in the printed proof, where Lean takes for N the last bound of Lemma I.2, it is stated for every pair of a first and a last state, and the exponent of Λ is the constant C of the statement. It also states what the program needs besides: the packets have at most T bits, at most T Λ bits start at a node, and the numbers of the program have room for packets, outcomes and pieces.

Theorem H.2, Proposition J.2 and Theorems J.3 and J.4 have the laws, and the last two the generators of A, as explicit standing hypotheses. The laws may be any finite family of laws, over any commutative ring, that has the properties of Theorem G.2, with h ≥ 3 and (G.1) as hypotheses; property (b) of Theorem G.2 enters as b ∑ e(λ + leni,e)2 ≤ G1 for an integer G1 ≤ 2C1a2 1. In the contracting case exists_laws and exists_generates supply these hypotheses, and exists_setting states the conclusion of Theorem J.4 without them. The programs of Theorem J.3 are written out in full, where we describe them (thm_onecut_evaluator, thm_onecut_program). The quotients in the bounds of Theorems J.3 and J.4 are rounded down in Lean.

Proposition K.5, Theorem K.6 and Proposition N.4 do not assume the contracting case. They take the conclusion of Theorem J.4 as a hypothesis (CutHyp), for a commutative ring A, which has to be finitely generated only in Theorem K.6 and Proposition N.4, and H = 16h with h ≥ 17, and scales_setting and prop_approx_acc_setting are their instances for the A and H of Section J in the contracting case.

In Section C Lean fixes one particular free ultrafilter, the one that Mathlib calls hyperfilter, and counts the prices Wn from n = 0; the Lean form of Lemma C.2 also asserts that the limit that defines N exists and equals the infimum. In Proposition M.2 Lean has HC0 = 1, which matters only for empty I. The theorem def_approx states when a circuit approximates a polynomial, as in the second sentence of Definition N.1; the last sentence of the definition is the definition of Paper.VPBar, and the match rests on reading it.

In Section I.1, Lean reads the construct of a pair from the length of its first component as a list, so that this component need not be the number of a construct, and such a pair is read as fail only if the length is above 10.

In Proposition I.1, that the two symbols of the word of an instance are different is a separate theorem (universal_symbols_ne). Lemma K.2 is stated for the alphabet of these two symbols and the end mark and with explicit constants, in which the time is O((d + 1) log(L + n) + (|z| + 1) log n); its bound on the number of steps is for accepting runs, and halting is stated for the z with |z| < n. In Lemma K.3, lem_circuit_phi states what is used of Φ, not that it equals the printed sum over words.
